pronunciation.ipaLabel: Conventional reading — Egyptian vocalisation not attested

phonemes.desc: The name is written wsjr; the initial w is a weak consonant (w or u) whose vowel is unwritten.
The god-determinative follows; the final r is consonantal. Egyptologists conventionally vocalise the name “Wesir”.

pronunciation.approximation: “WES-ir” — the form the Greeks heard as Ὄσιρις (Ósiris)
pronunciation.note: Egyptian hieroglyphs record consonants, not vowels; every vocalisation is a modern convention.

domains.title: God of the Dead, Resurrection, and the Nile’s Return
domains.subtitle: The First Mummy, King of the Underworld
domains.lead: Wsjr — Osiris to the Greeks — is the god who died and returned, and in returning became the pattern every Egyptian hoped to follow. Murdered by his brother, reassembled by his wife, enthroned as judge of the dead, he rules the Duat while his son Horus rules the living world above.

cards.name: King of the Duat
cards.desc: Sovereign of the underworld and judge of every soul weighed against the feather of Maat.

cards.name: The First Mummy
cards.desc: The drowned, dismembered god rewrapped by Anubis — the prototype of all mummification.

cards.name: The Green God
cards.desc: Lord of vegetation and the inundation; his green or black skin is the fertile flood-plain.

cards.name: Father of Horus
cards.desc: Posthumous father of the sky-falcon; the succession struggle with Seth is Egypt’s central myth.

mythology.lead: The Osiris cycle is the best-preserved Egyptian myth, known from the Pyramid Texts onward: the good king murdered by his brother, the faithful wife who recovers him, the son who avenges him. It is simultaneously a story about kingship, about the flood that dies and returns, and about every human being who hoped to be judged worthy.

myths.title: The Death of the Good King
myths.text: The earliest sources already presuppose the story: Osiris ruled as a beneficent king until his brother Seth, envious of his power, contrived his death — in the classical telling (Plutarch’s De Iside et Osiride, the fullest narrative we have) sealed in a chest and thrown into the Nile, the river carrying him to Byblos where a tamarisk grew to engulf the coffin.

myths.title: Isis the Faithful
myths.text: Isis searched for the body, recovered it from Byblos, and hid it — but Seth found it by night, cut it into fourteen pieces, and scattered them through Egypt. Isis and Nephthys wandered the land gathering the fragments. Every place that claimed a fragment became an Osiris sanctuary; the myth is a map of Egyptian pilgrimage.

myths.title: The Weighing of the Heart
myths.text: Anubis conducts the dead to the Hall of Two Truths, where the heart is set on the scale against the feather of Maat and the tally is read aloud by Thoth. Wsjr, enthroned in the next chamber, receives those who pass. The formula “I am Osiris” in the Book of the Dead identifies the deceased with him — his resurrection becomes the template of theirs.

myths.title: The Succession of Horus
myths.text: Isis, by magic, conceived a son on the briefly reanimated body: Horus, raised in secret in the marshes of Chemmis, who grew to challenge Seth for the throne. The tribunal of the gods awarded Egypt’s rule to Horus and the underworld’s to Osiris — the mythic charter for the division between the living king and his dead father.

lore.syncretism: Under the Ptolemies the Greeks mapped Osiris onto their own dying gods — Dionysus above all, whom Herodotus already calls “Osiris” — and the identification fed the later figure of Hellenistic Serapis. Through the Abydos cult his resurrection drew comparison with Christ in late-antique apologetics in both directions. The Coptic Church still preserves his name in ⲟⲩⲥⲓⲣⲉ as a theophoric element.
lore.culturalLegacy: Osiris gave the West its archetype of the dying-and-rising god and Egyptology one of its oldest debates: Frazer’s “Osiris as vegetation deity” reading dominated a century before J. Gwyn Griffiths and others restored his identity as dead king and judge. Abydos, his chief sanctuary, remained a pilgrimage goal for two millennia; the Osireion there, with its island surrounded by water, staged his myth in stone.
lore.extendedMeditation: The name on this temple is the consonantal skeleton the Egyptians themselves wrote — wsjr — because the vowels were never recorded and any vocalisation is an act of scholarship. That uncertainty is the point of the restoration: the god who embodies resurrection survives in a name we must partially reconstruct, held together by the determinative of a seated deity at the end of his own word.

sources.name: Pyramid Texts (Old Kingdom, utterances of the Osiris king)
Book of the Dead, spell 125 (the weighing of the heart)
Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride (the fullest narrative of the cycle)
Griffiths, The Origins of Osiris and his Cult

lore.archaeology: The Osireion at Abydos, excavated by Naville and Frankfort, is a cenotaph-temple flooded symbolically with groundwater; the Dynasty XIX temples of Seti I preserve the finest Osiris chapels and the Abydos King List. Fourteen supposed relic-sites of his body were listed by the Abydos and Mendes traditions, giving a physical geography to the dismemberment myth.
lore.cult: Abydos was the cult centre without rival, where the annual mysteries of Osiris staged the god’s death and revival with a processional boat (neshmet bark). Every dead person was ‘an Osiris’ — the name-title itself was the engine of personal religion, making the god’s cult indistinguishable from the Egyptian hope for the afterlife itself.
lore.iconography: Mummiform, arms crossed on the chest holding the crook and flail, wearing the tall white crown of Upper Egypt flanked by ostrich feathers; his skin is green or black — the colours of the flood-borne earth. As the Lunar deity he can be wrapped entirely as a moon-disc within a mummiform body, but the judge of the dead remains his definitive form.
lore.reception: Classical authors — Herodotus, Diodorus, Plutarch — transmitted the Osiris myth to Europe, where it shaped early theories of the ‘dying god’ and, through them, the modern study of religion itself. His weighing-of-the-heart scene, spell 125, is today the single most reproduced image of Egyptian religion, familiar far beyond scholarship.
